To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) positive contact in the past reduces the impact of negative contact on intergroup anxiety and (2) extensive contact in the past (i.e., contact across a range of situations) reduces the impact of contact on outgroup stereotyping.

(i) positive and diverse inter-group contact in the past reduces the impact of negative contact experiences on inter-group relations, (ii) the moderating role of past contact was observed in both face-to-face and imagined inter-group contact, and (iii) the moderating effects were observed in three conflict areas, Northern Ireland, the Arizona border area and Cyprus.
positive and extensive intergroup experience in the past buffers the negative effects of negative outgroup contact in the present on outgroup attitudes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of intergroup contact, and specifically the role of positive and negative contact, in the maintenance or change of intergroup relations, and the conditions under which contact has the potential to change intergroup attitudes and relations.
the role of history and the past in intergroup relations, and in particular, with the role of the past in moderating the impact of the present.
the impact of contact with outgroup members on the intergroup attitudes of individuals with positive and extensive intergroup histories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present research demonstrates a buffering effect of positive past contact experiences on the impact of negative contact experiences on intergroup relations.
the present study has demonstrated that the valence-salient contact effects are reduced or eliminated in the context of positive and extensive intergroup histories of contact.
positive contact in the past reduces the negative effects of negative contact in present.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more positive and extensive the intergroup contact, the more resilient people are against negative contact experiences.
the more positive intergroup contact people have had in the past, the less negative contact experiences in their present will affect them.
the positive and negative effects of intergroup contact depend on individuals' histories of intergroup contact.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of negative contact is moderated by individuals’ histories of contact.

positive and diverse contact experiences in the past may buffer against the negative impact of negative contact experiences, and that the negative impact of contact may be particularly pronounced for people who have limited or negative contact experiences.
intergroup contact in general is beneficial to intergroup relations.
